title: K-P-R
hookLine: kaparah, Yom Kippur: to cover over, to wipe clean

cards: "Make thee an ark of gopher wood." Noah gets his instructions: the wood, the rooms, the measurements. And one step that's easy to skip past.

Before the rain, before the animals, every seam has to be smeared with thick, dark pitch, inside and out, so the water can't get in. Sticky, unglamorous work. Without it, the ark is a very large box that sinks.
Keep that pot of pitch in view. Its Hebrew name shares three letters with a holy day. Kaf, fey, resh: K-P-R.

teach.b: Turn K-P-R four ways. First, the pitch. Noah "shalt pitch it within and without with pitch."
To pitch and the pitch both come from this root: kofer, a coating that covers. Second, the cover.
The ark of the covenant, the box that holds the tablets, gets a lid of pure gold called the kapporet, the ark-cover. On it, the text says, God will meet with Moses. A covering, and a holy one.
Yom Kippur, the day of atonements. Leviticus: "For on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you; from all your sins shall ye be clean before the LORD."
Hear both pictures: covering over, like pitch on a seam, and wiping clean. Fourth, the catch, which you met on day six hundred fifty-two.

teach.h: BETWEEN PEOPLE: GO TO THEM FIRST.
teach.b: The Mishnah, near the end of tractate Yoma, says: for wrongs between a person and God, Yom Kippur atones. For wrongs between one person and another, it does not, until the wrongdoer makes peace with the person they hurt.
The day can't do that part for you.
So before the fast, some people call each other, or knock on doors: I'm sorry for what I said in the spring. Atonement covers. But like Noah's pitch, it doesn't spread itself.
Someone has to pick up the brush and work it into the seam, one gap at a time.

how: Before Yom Kippur, Jews traditionally seek out people they may have wronged to ask forgiveness, following the Mishnah's teaching that the day atones for wrongs between people only once the wronged person has been appeased; the day itself is kept with fasting and prayer.

o: a root meaning to cover, and so atonement
a root meaning to confess, admitting a sin
a root meaning to fast, as on Yom Kippur

s: the root of Yom Kippur shows up in the story of Noah's ark
Noah pitches the ark with pitch, kofer, from K-P-R.
the Mishnah says Yom Kippur atones for wrongs against other people on its own
not until the wrongdoer makes peace with the person hurt.
the lid of the ark of the covenant shares the root of atonement

games.q: you snapped at a friend in the spring and never made it right. Yom Kippur comes, and you fast and pray. according to the Mishnah, is it covered?
o: not until you make peace with your friend.
only if your friend fasts too.
games.why: for wrongs between people, the Mishnah says the day does not atone until the one who did wrong makes peace with the one who was hurt.

practice: Bring to mind one small wrong you did that still has a gap in it, a word that stung, a call you didn't return, a favor you let drop, and picture the person.
Then picture one good thing that could cover that seam: an apology, plain and specific, a call, the favor done late. Choose it, and if you pray, bring that person into the quiet.

wordCard.voice: K-P-R. Kaf, fey, resh: kofer, the pitch on Noah's ark; kapporet, the ark-cover; kaparah, atonement, as in Yom Kippur. To cover over, to wipe clean. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: atonement; from K-P-R, to cover, as in Yom Kippur.

carryVoice: Your line: atonement covers. Between people, the covering starts with the person you hurt. Go gently.
